title: La Salle Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: La Salle wells have a 48-foot median depth, with typical completed well costs of $8,400-$15,400.
h1: What Wells Are Like Around La Salle, Colorado
intro_html:
La Salle sits on the plains in Weld County, where permitted wells are commonly shallow and many records identify Denver Basin aquifers or alluvial materials. Within 5 miles of town, Colorado DWR records include 2,945 wells, although fewer records report construction, yield, or static water level. That matters when you compare a property to nearby permits: the local numbers are useful for setting expectations, but they do not guarantee what a new hole will produce.

For a purchase or building project, look at depth, documented yield, water level, permit type, septic layout, and nearby environmental sites together. The records around La Salle include Evans, Garden City, Greeley, Gilcrest, Kersey, and Milliken, giving a broader local comparison than a single parcel can provide.

sections.heading: La Salle wells are usually shallow
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near La Salle is 48 feet. The middle half runs from 25 to 72 feet, and 90% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Another 9% fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 1% reach from 300 to 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 600 feet.

That distribution is useful when reviewing a drilling estimate. A bid near the local median depth is not unusual, but a parcel can still require a deeper hole because of its exact geology, the selected aquifer, casing and grout requirements, or the intended use. The records identify 1,951 wells as unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer wells, 469 as Alluvial, and 81 as Quaternary Alluvium. Denver Basin aquifers account for 71% of named permit records.

sections.heading: Most reported La Salle wells make useful flow
sections.html:
Yield records are strong on paper, but only 277 wells report a pump yield. Among those records, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15.0 to 800.0 gallons per minute. Eighty-three percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, 14% report from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 3% report from 1 to 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures describe tested records, not a promise for an unbuilt well. Ask for the actual pumping test, recovery information, permit limitations, and intended household demand. A domestic permit is different from an irrigation or stock-water use. Colorado exempt household-use wells also have legal limits, including the 35-gpm pumping limit, so a high-yield record does not automatically mean unrestricted water use.

sections.heading: Water levels are close to the surface here
sections.html:
Reported static water levels near La Salle have a median depth of 12 feet below the surface. The middle half is from 5 to 19 feet. That shallow water level can reduce pumping lift, but it also means construction and surface drainage deserve careful attention. A shallow water table is not the same as safe drinking water.

The decade series does not show a simple continuing decline. The median measured depth was 20 feet in the 1960s, 7 feet in the 2000s, 12 feet in the 2010s, and 10 feet in the 2020s. Measurement locations, seasons, well construction, and aquifer conditions can differ, so use the series as local context rather than a parcel-specific forecast. Only 243 records report a static water level, limiting how broadly it can be applied.

sections.heading: Permit activity has picked up in La Salle
sections.html:
Permit records show long-running well development around La Salle. Permits issued by decade include 154 in the 1950s, 194 in the 1960s, 147 in the 1970s, 131 in the 1980s, 366 in the 1990s, 249 in the 2000s, 278 in the 2010s, and 517 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

The most active drillers listed are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 750 records; Clement, Glenn A., with 178; and Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed), with 102. These names help when searching historic permits or asking a seller for completion reports. They do not establish current availability, pricing, or a recommendation. Confirm the permit status and water right with Colorado DWR before relying on an old record.

sections.heading: What a new La Salle well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 48-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $2,400 to $3,400. That is not the complete project price.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,400 to $15,400. The final bid can change with access, casing and grout, difficult ground, distance to the building, power installation, water testing, and the permit requirements for the property. Ask the driller to separate drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and any standby or dry-hole charges. A short local well can still have substantial completion costs.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space, and dry-hole risk
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information deserves review before buying. Within about 10 miles of La Salle, the records show 2,599 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove contamination at a specific parcel, but they are a reason to test the well and understand nearby land uses, groundwater direction, and any recorded advisories.

Low yield is not the only risk. A driller can encounter different materials than nearby wells, and fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable. Confirm the permit allows the planned use, locate the proposed well away from septic components, and leave room for the building, access, electrical service, and replacement equipment. For a new home, review augmentation requirements if the basin or permit calls for them. A well test and laboratory water test should be conditions of the purchase when records are limited.

faq.q: How deep are wells in La Salle, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth near La Salle is 48 feet. The middle half of wells runs from 25 to 72 feet, and 90% are under 100 feet. Some are much deeper: 9% are from 100 to 300 feet, 1% are from 300 to 600 feet, and the deepest record is 600 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in La Salle?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 48-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,400 to $3,400. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $8,400 to $15,400. Access, geology, casing, grout, and site layout can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do La Salle wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 277 local wells that report pump yield, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 800.0 gallons per minute. Records show 83% above 15 gallons per minute, but that applies only to reported tests and does not guarantee the result for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in La Salle?
faq.a: A shallow water level or strong yield does not prove drinking-water safety. The area has 2,599 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, plus other environmental records. Test the specific well through a qualified laboratory and review nearby land uses, septic systems, permits, and any Colorado DWR or public-health information before drinking the water.

faq.q: Are La Salle wells getting deeper or water levels dropping?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 20 feet below the surface in the 1960s, 7 feet in the 2000s, 12 feet in the 2010s, and 10 feet in the 2020s. That series does not show a simple continuing decline. Only 243 wells report static levels, so use the trend as background rather than a prediction for a specific lot.
